words.title: Celerity
words.definition: Swiftness of movement; rapidity of action or motion.
words.etymology: From Latin **celeritas** (swiftness), from *celer* (swift, quick). Entered English in the late 15th century. The adjective form *celeritous* is rare; the more common relative is *accelerate* — both trace to the same root *celer*.
words.example: The board was urged to proceed with **celerity** on the matter rather than letting it drag on.
words.memoryHook: **Celerity** shares its Latin root with **accelerate** — so anything moving with celerity is accelerating. The "celer" in both words is the same *swift*.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Alician
words.definition: Surreal, whimsical, or illogical.
words.etymology: From **Alice**, heroine of Lewis Carroll's *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland* (1865) and *Through the Looking-Glass* (1871).
words.example: The meeting took an **Alician** turn when the agenda stopped making sense entirely.
words.memoryHook: **Alician** = like falling down the rabbit hole — rules keep shifting.
related: frabjous — Carroll's own coinage from the Looking-Glass poems

words.title: Allopatric
words.definition: Existing or occurring in geographically distinct areas.
words.etymology: From **allo-** (other) + Greek *patra* (fatherland); coined in the context of speciation biology.
words.example: **Allopatric** species evolve in isolation, each adapting to its own corner of the map.
words.memoryHook: *Allo-* (other) + *patra* (fatherland) → **allopatric** = dwelling in a different land.
related: furcate — both terms about natural division and branching

words.title: Amerce
words.definition: To punish with a fine set at the court's discretion.
words.etymology: From Middle English **amercien**, from Anglo-Norman French *amercier* (to fine), from the phrase *estre a merci* — "to be at the mercy" of another. The name is the whole mechanism: an amercement had no fixed tariff, so the offender stood at the mercy of the court for the sum. First documented use: 14th century. The noun is *amercement*; the adjective, *amerciable*.
words.example: A villager caught poaching could be **amerced** at whatever sum the lord's court thought fitting.
words.memoryHook: *A merci* = "at the mercy." To be **amerced** is to be fined whatever the court's mercy decides — the same *merci* as the French for thank you, and as *mercy* itself.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Avuncular
words.definition: Kind, friendly, and helpful, like an uncle, in a benevolent or indulgent way.
words.etymology: From Latin **avunculus** (maternal uncle), diminutive of *avus* (grandfather).
words.example: The old foreman had an **avuncular** manner, gruff but quick to look out for the new hires.
words.memoryHook: *Avunculus* = maternal uncle → **avuncular** = uncle-like warmth and good humor.
related: propinquity — another kinship-flavored word
matronymic — *avunculus* is the maternal uncle; both words track the mother's line

words.title: Bombinate
words.definition: To buzz; to hum.
words.etymology: From Latin **bombinare** / *bombilare* (to buzz), from *bombus* (a humming, buzzing).
words.example: Her head had become a **bombinating** vacuum after hours of close reading.
words.memoryHook: *Bombus* = the Latin for a buzz, and the genus of bumblebees → to **bombinate** is to buzz like a bee.
related: cachinnate — another Latin verb built from the sound it names
obganiate — from *gannire*, a dog's yelp; imitative in the same way

words.title: Cachinnate
words.definition: To laugh loudly or immoderately.
words.etymology: From Latin **cachinnare** (to laugh loudly), of imitative origin — the word *is* the sound of the laugh. First documented use: 1824. Old English, Old High German, and Greek each coined their own imitative words for boisterous laughter; *giggle* and *guffaw* were made the same way, from different roots.
words.example: He **cachinnated** at his own punchline until the rest of the table went quiet.
words.memoryHook: Latin *cachinnare* is onomatopoeia — *kah-kah-kah*, the laugh itself. Same trick as **bombinate**, where *bombus* is the buzz.
related: bombinate — another Latin verb built from the sound it names
obganiate — from *gannire*, a dog's yelp; imitative in the same way

words.title: Commensurate
words.definition: Corresponding in size or degree; in proportion.
words.etymology: From Late Latin **commensuratus**, from *com-* (with) + *mensura* (measure).
words.example: Your salary should be **commensurate** with the weight of the responsibility you carry.
words.memoryHook: *Com-* (together) + *mensura* (measure) → things **commensurate** are measured on the same scale.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Cumberworld
words.definition: A useless person.
words.etymology: From **cumber** (to burden, hinder) + *world*. Middle English.
words.example: The old proverb called an idle dependent a **cumberworld** — a burden nobody wanted.
words.memoryHook: **Cumber** (to burden) + **world** → someone who only encumbers the world.
related: nous — the practical sense a cumberworld conspicuously lacks

words.title: Desistance
words.definition: The act of ceasing a behavior, particularly one considered harmful or unwanted.
words.etymology: From Old French **desister**, from Latin *desistere* (to leave off), from *de-* + *sistere* (to stand).
words.example: Studies of criminal **desistance** show that stable work often predicts a drop in offending.
words.memoryHook: *De-* (down/away) + *sistere* (to stand) → to stop standing there; **desistance** = the act of stopping.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Diachronic
words.definition: Relating to changes occurring over time.
words.etymology: From French **diachronique**, from *dia-* (across) + Greek *khronos* (time).
words.example: A **diachronic** study of the language traces how its grammar shifted across centuries.
words.memoryHook: *Dia-* (across) + *chronos* (time) → **diachronic** = across time. The opposite, *synchronic*, is at one point in time.
related: senescent — change over time applied to aging

words.title: Disject
words.definition: To scatter or disperse.
words.etymology: From Latin **disjicere** (to scatter), from *dis-* (apart) + *jacere* (to throw). First documented use: 1581.
words.example: Can a storm ever be calmer than the stillness it **disjects**?
words.memoryHook: *Dis-* (apart) + *jacere* (throw) → **disject** = throw apart, scatter.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Éclat
words.definition: Enthusiastic approval; a strikingly brilliant display; notable success.
words.etymology: From French **éclat** (splinter, brilliance), from *éclater* (to burst out) — the same root that gave us *slat* and *eclair*. First documented use: 1676.
words.example: The journal published the hoax with great **éclat**, only to retract it in embarrassment.
words.memoryHook: *Éclat* literally "splinters" like light off a jewel — brilliance that shatters attention.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Empyrean
words.definition: Relating to heaven or the sky; the highest heaven.
words.etymology: From Greek **empyros** (in fire), from *en* (in) + *pyr* (fire). In medieval cosmology the empyrean was the highest heaven of pure fire and light.
words.example: The **empyrean** domain where human will and God's will became as one.
words.memoryHook: *Pyro* = fire in Greek → **empyrean** = "in fire," the blazing highest heaven.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Fabulist
words.definition: A creator or writer of fables; a liar.
words.etymology: From Middle French **fabuliste**, from Latin *fabula* (a story, a tale), from *fari* (to speak) — the same root behind *fable*, *fabulous*, and *infant* (one not yet speaking). First documented use: 1593. The slide from sense 1 to sense 2 is the whole word: a fable is a story that never happened, so the teller of fables became the teller of untruths.
words.example: Half the anecdotes in the memoir turned out to be invented, and the reviewers began calling him a **fabulist**.
words.memoryHook: A **fabulist** writes *fables* — and a fable is a story that isn't true, which is exactly how the same word came to mean *liar*.
related: nefandous — from the same Latin root *fari* (to speak)
veracious — the truthfulness a fabulist lacks
indite — another word for the act of composing
mendacious — the adjective for what a fabulist does in sense 2

words.title: Frowze
words.definition: To make untidy, tangled, or ruffled; a wig of frizzed hair.
words.etymology: Origin unknown. First documented use: 1563.
words.example: The wind **frowzed** her hair into a halo of tangles before the interview.
words.memoryHook: Sounds like "frowsy" (unkempt) → **frowze** = to make frowsy.
related: frowzy — the adjective of the same unknown-origin family

words.title: Furcate
words.definition: To divide into two or more branches; forked.
words.etymology: From Late Latin **furcatus** (forked), from *furca* (fork).
words.example: The river **furcates** around the island before rejoining downstream.
words.memoryHook: A *furca* is a pitchfork → to **furcate** is to split like a fork's tines.
related: allopatric — both terms for geographic/natural division

words.title: Imbroglio
words.definition: A difficult, confusing, or embarrassing situation; a confused heap or tangle.
words.etymology: From Italian **imbroglio** (confusion), from *imbrogliare* (to tangle), from *in-* + *broglio* (tangle).
words.example: The contract dispute turned into a legal **imbroglio** no one could untangle.
words.memoryHook: Italian for "tangle" — an **imbroglio** is a knot of complications.
related: welter — another word for a confused mass

words.title: Indefatigable
words.definition: Incapable of being tired out; persistently energetic and tireless.
words.etymology: From Latin **indefatigabilis**, from *in-* (not) + *defatigare* (to tire out).
words.example: She was an **indefatigable** advocate, still making calls at midnight long after others had quit.
words.memoryHook: *In-* (not) + *defatigare* (to tire) → **indefatigable** = cannot be fatigued.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Indite
words.definition: To compose or write; to put down in writing; to give literary or formal expression to.
words.etymology: From Latin **indictare** (to proclaim), from *indicere* (to proclaim, declare). An etymological cognate of *indict*: both share the Latin root, but *indict* shifted meaning via Anglo-French legal usage to "to formally accuse or charge with a crime," while *indite* kept the original sense of writing and composing.
words.example: The lawyer was asked to **indite** a formal response to the complaint.
words.memoryHook: To **indite** is to "dictate" words onto the page; its twin *indict* splits off into the courtroom (to accuse), while *indite* stays at the writing desk.
related: fabulist — one who composes fables
verso — the page the writing lands on
prolegomenon — a formal essay indited to introduce a longer work

words.title: Lachrymose
words.definition: Tearful or given to weeping; inducing tears, mournful.
words.etymology: From Latin **lacrimosus** (tearful), from *lacrima* (a tear) — the same root as the *lachrymal* glands that produce them. First documented use: 1727, though Oxford dates an earlier sense, "like tears; liable to exude in drops," to the mid-17th century. The *ch* is a later Latinate flourish; the Latin has no *h* in it.
words.example: The last twenty minutes turn **lachrymose** in a way the rest of the film has earned no right to be.
words.memoryHook: *Lacrima* = tear → **lachrymose** = full of tears, and the *lachrymal* glands are where they come from.
related: melpomenish — tragedy, the thing that makes an audience lachrymose

words.title: Melpomenish
words.definition: Tragic; related to tragedy.
words.etymology: From **Melpomene**, the Greek muse of tragedy.
words.example: The third act had a **melpomenish** weight that left the audience silent.
words.memoryHook: Melpomene is the **tragedy** muse; her sister Thalia is comedy → **melpomenish** = tragic.
related: penelopean — another word from Greek mythology
lachrymose — the tears tragedy is meant to draw
corybantic — another adjective coined from Greek myth

words.title: Mendacious
words.definition: Not telling the truth; lying, especially as a habit.
words.etymology: From Latin **mendax** (*mendac-*, lying), from *menda* (a fault, a defect). First documented use: 1616. The same *mend-* root gives *amend* and *emend* — literally to take the fault out. Latin *mendax* was later coloured by *mentiri* (to speak falsely), which pulled it from "defective" toward "deceitful." Compared with *lying*, **mendacious** is the formal, literary word, and describes a character trait more than an act.
words.example: The report was not merely mistaken but **mendacious** — the numbers had been chosen, not found.
words.memoryHook: Latin *menda* = a fault → a **mendacious** account has the fault built in on purpose. Its cousin *amend* takes the fault back out.
related: veracious — the direct opposite, from *verus* (true)
fabulist — a teller of fables, in the pejorative sense
perfidious — deceit aimed at betraying trust

words.title: Mimetic
words.definition: Copying the behavior, appearance, or characteristics of others.
words.etymology: From Greek **mimetikos** (imitation), from *mimesis*, from *mimeisthai* (to imitate). First documented use: 1632.
words.example: Fashion is a **mimetic** loop — designers copy each other and the public copies them.
words.memoryHook: Think *mime* — a performer who copies — plus the -*etic* suffix → **mimetic** = mime-like imitation.
related: zugunruhe — another word about inherited behavior

words.title: Minacious
words.definition: Threatening or menacing.
words.etymology: From Latin **minari** (to threaten), from *minae* (threats) — ultimately from the Indo-European root *men-* (project), also the source of *menace*, *mountain*, *eminent*, *promenade*, *demean*, *amenable*, and *mouth*. First documented use: 1660. A synonym is *minatory*.
words.example: The gathering clouds had a **minacious** look that hurried the farmers inside.
words.memoryHook: *Minae* = threats in Latin → **minacious** = threat-heavy. Same root as *menace* and *mountain*.
related: timorous — the fearful response to a threat

words.title: Multifarious
words.definition: Many and of various types; having many varied parts or aspects.
words.etymology: From Latin **multifarius** (manyfold), from *multus* (many) + *-farius*.
words.example: The committee's **multifarious** activities made a single report impossible to write.
words.memoryHook: *Multi-* (many) + *farious* (fold) → **multifarious** = many-fold, many kinds.
related: salmagundi — the noun for a many-and-various collection

words.title: Nefandous
words.definition: So wicked as to defy description; abominable, appalling.
words.etymology: From Latin **nefandus** (wicked), from *ne-* (not) + *fandus* (to be spoken), the gerundive of *fari* (to speak). First documented use: 1649.
words.example: The historian called the massacre **nefandous** — a crime too foul for words.
words.memoryHook: *Ne-* (not) + *fandus* (to be spoken) → **nefandous** = not to be spoken of, unutterably evil.
related: perfidious — another word for moral evil
turpitude — a noun for depravity
fabulist — from the same Latin root *fari* (to speak)
parrhesia — its exact inverse: speech that holds nothing back

words.title: Nous
words.definition: Common sense; practical intelligence. In philosophy, the mind or intellect.
words.etymology: From Greek **nous** (*noos*) — mind, intelligence, intuitive apprehension. First documented use: 1678. It arrived in English as a technical term of philosophy and only later picked up the informal British sense of street-level practical wit, which is now the commoner of the two. Britons rhyme it with *house*; Americans often say *NOOS*.
words.example: She had every credential on paper and not enough **nous** to see the deal was collapsing under her.
words.memoryHook: Greek *nous* = mind. Someone who "hasn't got the **nous**" for a job hasn't got the *mind* for it.
related: cumberworld — a useless person is precisely one with no nous

words.title: Penelopean
words.definition: Involving repetitive or cyclical efforts, often with little apparent progress; steadfast loyalty and resilience.
words.etymology: From **Penelope**, Odysseus's wife, who held off suitors by weaving a shroud each day and secretly unraveling it each night.
words.example: Rehab felt **Penelopean** — every gain seemed undone by morning, yet she kept at it.
words.memoryHook: Penelope **weaves by day and unravels by night** → work that resets, plus the loyalty to keep going.
related: melpomenish — another word from Greek mythology
corybantic — Greek myth again, and the opposite temper: frenzy against patient repetition

words.title: Perfidious
words.definition: Treacherous; deceitful; betraying trust.
words.etymology: From Latin **perfidus** (treacherous), from *per-* (beyond) + *fidus* (faith). First documented use: 1538.
words.example: A **perfidious** ally smiled to your face and sold your plans by night.
words.memoryHook: *Per-* (through/beyond) + *fides* (faith) → one who has gone **past** faith is **perfidious**.
related: nefandous — another word for moral evil
turpitude — a noun for depravity
mendacious — habitual lying, a quieter cousin of treachery

words.title: Pluvial
words.definition: Relating to or characterized by rainfall.
words.etymology: From Latin **pluvialis**, from *pluvia* (rain).
words.example: The alternation of **pluvial** and arid periods shaped the region's ancient climate.
words.memoryHook: *Pluvia* is Latin for rain → **pluvial** = rainy. Picture "pluie," French for rain.
related: rupestrian — another Latin adjective for the physical landscape

words.title: Propinquity
words.definition: The state of being close to someone or something; proximity; close kinship.
words.etymology: From Latin **propinquitas**, from *propinquus* (near), from *prope* (near).
words.example: He kept his distance, as though afraid **propinquity** might lead him into temptation.
words.memoryHook: *Prope* = near in Latin → **propinquity** = nearness. "Propinquity breeds affection."
related: avuncular — another kinship-flavored word
matronymic — kinship recorded in a name
chumocracy — nepotism runs on kinship, chumocracy on friendship

words.title: Rupestrian
words.definition: Composed of rock; inscribed or painted on rocks.
words.etymology: From New Latin **rupestris** (of rock), from Latin *rupes* (rock, cliff) + *-estris*, the ending seen in *terrestris* (of the earth). *Rupes* traces back to *rumpere* (to break) — a cliff is the earth broken open. First documented use: 1809. The variant *rupestral* means the same thing.
words.example: The canyon walls held **rupestrian** figures painted centuries before anyone farmed the valley.
words.memoryHook: Latin *rupes* (rock) wearing the *-estrian* ending of **equestrian** and **pedestrian** → **rupestrian** = of the rock.
related: pluvial — another Latin adjective for the physical landscape
boscage — thicket rather than rock; the folder's other terrain noun

words.title: Senescent
words.definition: Growing old; aging; deteriorating with the passage of time.
words.etymology: From Latin **senescere** (to grow old), from *senex* (old).
words.example: The once-vibrant orchard had gone **senescent**, its branches brittle and half bare.
words.memoryHook: *Senex* = old man in Latin → **senescent** = aging. The prefix *sen-* signals old age.
related: diachronic — change over time, of which aging is one kind
fugacious — the opposite tempo: gone quickly rather than declining slowly

words.title: Surfeit
words.definition: An excessive amount of something; to cause someone to desire no more.
words.etymology: From Old French **surfaire** (to overdo), from *sur-* (over) + *faire* (to do), from Latin *superfacere*.
words.example: I am **surfeited** with shopping — one more store and I'll crack.
words.memoryHook: *Sur-* (over) + *faire* (to do) → to **surfeit** is to do or consume past the point of want.
related: (none in folder)

words.title: Timorous
words.definition: Showing or suffering from nervousness, fear, or a lack of confidence.
words.etymology: From Old French **temoreus**, from Medieval Latin *timorosus*, from Latin *timor* (fear), from *timere* (to fear).
words.example: He asked the question in a **timorous** voice, expecting the answer he feared.
words.memoryHook: *Timor* is Latin for fear → **timorous** = full of fear. Think "timid."
related: minacious — the threatening flip side of fearful

words.title: Turpitude
words.definition: Depravity; wickedness.
words.etymology: From Latin **turpitudo** (baseness), from *turpis* (vile, base).
words.example: The nominee was rejected over acts of moral **turpitude** from his past.
words.memoryHook: *Turpis* = base/vile in Latin → **turpitude** = baseness. Think "moral turpitude."
related: perfidious — a treacherous form of wickedness
nefandous — unspeakable wickedness
chumocracy — the institutional form it often takes
anomie — depravity breaks the standard; anomie is having none to break

words.title: Veracious
words.definition: Speaking or representing the truth; truthful.
words.etymology: From Latin **verax** (truthful), from *verus* (true).
words.example: The memoir was praised as a **veracious** account of the war, down to the smallest detail.
words.memoryHook: *Verus* = true in Latin → **veracious** = truthful. Compare its sibling **verity**.
related: verity — the noun form of the same root
fabulist — a teller of fables; in its second sense, the opposite
mendacious — the direct opposite, already listed in its antonyms
parrhesia — truth-telling as a public act, and a risky one

words.title: Verity
words.definition: The quality of being true; a universally accepted truth.
words.etymology: From Latin **veritas** (truth), from *verus* (true).
words.example: Some **verities** — that power corrupts, that time wounds all heels — never lose their force.
words.memoryHook: *Verus* = true → **verity** = truth. Compare its adjective sibling **veracious**.
related: veracious — the adjective from the same root

words.title: Verso
words.definition: The side of a leaf that is to be read second; a left-hand page.
words.etymology: From New Latin **verso** (*folio*), "the leaf having been turned" — the ablative of *versus*, past participle of Latin *vertere* (to turn). The same root gives *reverse*, *invert*, *divert*, and *vertigo*. Its counterpart is *recto*, the right-hand page, from *recto folio*, "the leaf being straight." First documented use: 1839.
words.example: The illustration ran across the **verso**, leaving the recto free for the text.
words.memoryHook: *Verso folio* = "the leaf having been turned." Same *vertere* as *reverse* — turn the page and you land on the **verso**.
related: indite — another word from the writer's desk
prolegomenon — another term from the anatomy of the book

words.title: Welter
words.definition: To move in a turbulent fashion; a confused mass or state of disorder.
words.etymology: From Middle English **welteren**, from Middle Dutch / Low German *welteren* (to roll, tumble).
words.example: The attack petered out in a **welter** of bloody, confused fighting.
words.memoryHook: To **welter** is to wallow and roll — chaos that thrashes around.
related: imbroglio — another word for a confused tangle
salmagundi — the same heap of unlike things, arranged and served
anomie — disorder in a society's rules rather than in a scene

words.title: Zugunruhe
words.definition: Restlessness at the beginning of a migration period.
words.etymology: From German **Zugunruhe**: *Zug* (migration) + *Unruhe* (restlessness). First documented use: 1950.
words.example: Captive birds start to pace and flutter with **zugunruhe** weeks before their wild kin leave.
words.memoryHook: *Zug* = "train" moving, *Unruhe* = unease → the animal's restless itch to get moving.
related: mimetic — another word about inherited behavior
solivagant — the one who acts on the restlessness, alone

words.title: Corybantic
words.definition: Wild; frenzied, in the manner of ecstatic ritual dance.
words.etymology: From the **Corybantes** (Greek *Korybantes*), the attendant priests of Cybele, the Phrygian "Great Mother of the Gods," who worshipped her with wildly emotional processions and dancing. First documented use: 1642. The Corybantes were often conflated with the Curetes, who in myth clashed their shields to drown out the infant Zeus's cries — in both stories the noise and the frenzy are the point.
words.example: By the encore the floor had gone **corybantic**, a thousand people moving as one animal.
words.memoryHook: The **Corybantes** worshipped by dancing themselves into a frenzy → **corybantic** = that kind of wild.
related: melpomenish — another adjective coined from Greek myth
penelopean — likewise, and its opposite in temper: patient repetition against ecstatic frenzy

words.title: Solivagant
words.definition: A solitary wanderer; wandering alone.
words.etymology: From Latin **solivagus** (wandering alone), from *solus* (alone) + *vagus* (wandering). First documented use: 1621. *Vagus* is the productive half of the compound: it also gives *vague*, *vagrant*, *vagabond*, and *extravagant* (literally "wandering beyond") — and the *vagus nerve*, so named because it wanders farther from the brain than any other cranial nerve.
words.example: Three days in he had peeled off from the group, happily **solivagant** along the coast road.
words.memoryHook: *Solus* (alone) + *vagus* (wandering) → a **solivagant** wanders solo. Same *vagus* as the nerve that wanders the length of the torso.
related: zugunruhe — the restlessness that precedes the wandering

words.title: Boscage
words.definition: A growth of trees or shrubs; a grove, thicket, or underwood.
words.etymology: From Anglo-French **boscage** (wood, woodland), from *bois*, *bosc* (grove, forest) + *-age*, from Medieval Latin *boscus* (grove) — which is itself probably Germanic, the same stock as English *bush*. First documented use: 15th century. The root is unusually productive: it gives Italian *bosco*, Spanish *bosque*, French *bois*, English *bosky*, and — by way of the Picard diminutive *boschet* — **bouquet**, which entered English in 1716 meaning "little wood." *Ambush* belongs to the family too: to lie in wait in the bushes.
words.example: Beyond the last fence the trail gave out entirely and vanished into dense **boscage**.
words.memoryHook: The same *bosc-* (wood) that gives *bouquet* — literally a "little wood" of flowers — and *ambush*, hiding in one. **Boscage** is the wood itself.
related: rupestrian — the folder's other word for a specific kind of terrain

words.title: Frowzy
words.definition: Scruffy and neglected in appearance; dingy, musty, and stuffy.
words.etymology: Late 17th century, originally dialect; origin unknown. First documented use: 1681. Etymonline suggests a link to dialectal *frowsty* (having an unpleasant smell), itself of uncertain parentage — possibly Old French *frouste* (ruinous, decayed) or Old English *þroh* (rancid). **Frowsy** is the commoner spelling in American dictionaries; *frowzy* is the variant Oxford leads with. Note the two senses run on different senses of the body: one is what a place *looks* like, the other what it *smells* like.
words.example: The lobby had gone **frowzy** — dim, overwarm, and smelling faintly of the carpet's last thirty years.
words.memoryHook: It rhymes with *drowsy*, and it describes exactly what a room looks like after a long one. Same murky family as **frowze**, to make untidy.
related: frowze — the verb of the same unknown-origin family; to make frowzy

words.title: Parrhesia
words.definition: Boldness or freedom of speech; candid speech that risks something in the telling.
words.etymology: From Greek **parrhesia**, from *pan* (all) + *rhesis* (speech, utterance) — literally "saying everything." It reached English through Medieval Latin. *Rhesis* traces to *eirein* (to say), the same root behind *rhetoric*, which makes the pair neatly opposed: rhetoric is the art of how you say it, parrhesia is saying it anyway. Merriam-Webster carries the word but publishes no First Known Use; it is in English rhetoric handbooks by the late 16th century, where Henry Peacham lists *Parrhesia* among the "figures of permission" in *The Garden of Eloquence*.
words.example: What the board wanted was consensus; what the auditor gave them was **parrhesia**.
words.memoryHook: *Pan* (all) + *rhesis* (speech) → **parrhesia** = saying all of it, holding nothing back — and taking the consequences.
related: nefandous — its exact inverse: what is *not* to be spoken
veracious — the truth-telling that parrhesia performs out loud

words.title: Matronymic
words.definition: A name derived from the name of a mother or female ancestor; of or relating to such a name.
words.etymology: A hybrid word: Latin *matr-* (mother) grafted onto the *-onymic* of **patronymic**, which is Greek all the way down — *patronymos* (named from the father), from *pater* (father) + *onyma* (name). First documented use: 1794 as a noun, 1874 as an adjective; *patronymic* beat it into English by nearly two centuries (1610s). Purists who dislike the Latin-Greek splice prefer **metronymic**, built cleanly from Greek *meter* (mother) — the two words mean the same thing, and the ugly one won.
words.example: Icelandic naming is overwhelmingly patronymic, but a child registered under a **matronymic** takes the mother's name instead: Guðrún's daughter becomes Guðrúnardóttir.
words.memoryHook: *Matr-* (mother) + *onyma* (name) → the mother's name carried forward. Its tidier twin *metronymic* is fully Greek; **matronymic** is the mongrel that stuck.
related: avuncular — from *avunculus*, specifically the *maternal* uncle; both words track the mother's line
propinquity — the folder's other word for kinship and nearness

words.title: Obganiate
words.definition: To annoy someone by repeatedly saying the same thing; to repeat oneself tediously.
words.etymology: Irregularly formed on Latin **obgannire** (also *oggannire*), to yelp or growl at, from *ob-* (at, against) + *gannire* (to yelp, snarl, whine — what a dog does). First documented use: 1623. Merriam-Webster has no entry for it at all; the OED carries one, and the date comes from A.Word.A.Day. The English form is a botch — *obgannire* has two *n*'s and the English word only one — which is presumably why the word never caught on despite naming something everybody has endured.
words.example: He had one grievance about the parking and would **obganiate** about it at every meeting until people stopped making eye contact.
words.memoryHook: Latin *gannire* is a dog's yelp; *ob-* means *at*. To **obganiate** is to yelp *at* somebody — the same complaint, over and over, until they'd rather you just barked.
related: cachinnate — another Latin verb built from the sound it names
bombinate — the third of the imitative Latin verbs in this folder

words.title: Anomie
words.definition: Social instability from a breakdown of standards and values; the personal alienation that follows.
words.etymology: Borrowed from French **anomie**, from Greek *anomia* (lawlessness), from *a-* (without) + *nomos* (law, custom) — from the Proto-Indo-European root **nem-** (to assign, allot), which also gives *autonomy*, *economy*, and *astronomy*. First documented use: 1933, though Etymonline dates the reborrowed French spelling to 1915; the older anglicized form *anomy*, meaning "lawlessness, violation of divine law," was in English by the 1590s. Émile Durkheim supplied the modern meaning in *Le Suicide* (1897) — not crime, but the condition of a society whose rules have stopped binding, and the vertigo of the people living inside it. The variant spelling *anomy* survives, barely.
words.example: He described the town after the plant closed less as poverty than as **anomie** — nobody could say any longer what a good life there was supposed to look like.
words.memoryHook: *A-* (without) + *nomos* (law) → **anomie** = no rules left to steer by. Not lawbreaking; law*lessness*.
related: welter — disorder you can see; anomie is disorder in the rules themselves
turpitude — depravity is breaking the standard; anomie is having none to break

words.title: Chumocracy
words.definition: A government, organization, or culture in which friends and associates are favored, especially in appointments to authority.
words.etymology: From **chum** (friend) + *-ocracy* (rule), from Greek *kratos* (power, strength). *Chum* is 1680s Oxford university slang, apparently a clipped form of *cham*, itself short for *chamber-mate* or *chamber fellow* — a roommate, in an era fond of lopping words short. First documented use: 1937, and the coinage was sunny: a Delaware newspaper column reported a fellowship order hoping to "establish Chumocracy through the breadth and length of the land." It was reborn as an insult in the British press in 1992, aimed at John Major's cabinet, and again in the 2020s over pandemic contracts steered to ministers' friends.
words.example: Three of the four appointees had shared a staircase at university, which told you all you needed to know about the **chumocracy** running the place.
words.memoryHook: *Chum* (roommate) + *-cracy* (rule) → **chumocracy** = government by the people you shared a room with. Nepotism is the relatives; chumocracy is the friends.
related: propinquity — nearness and kinship: what nepotism runs on, where chumocracy runs on friendship
turpitude — the moral register a chumocracy usually earns

words.title: Salmagundi
words.definition: A miscellaneous mixture or collection; originally a composed salad of chopped meat, anchovies, eggs, and onions.
words.etymology: From French **salmigondis** (16th century), earlier *salmigondin*, of uncertain origin — possibly Latin *sal* (salt) + *condire* (to season, flavor), and probably tangled with Old French *salemine* (a hodgepodge of meats or fish cooked in wine), which Middle English had already borrowed as *salomene* by the early 14th century. First documented use: c. 1674. The dish came first; the figurative "mixture of various ingredients" followed by 1761. Washington Irving then used *Salmagundi* as the title of his satirical magazine of 1807–08, which is how the word lodged itself in American English. English mouths never quite settled it — the dialect forms *salmon-gundy* and *solomon-gundy* both survived.
words.example: The estate sale was a **salmagundi** of ship models, tax records, and a single unexplained taxidermied heron.
words.memoryHook: Probably *sal* (salt) + *condire* (to season) → a salted, seasoned jumble on a plate. Any pile of unlike things is now a **salmagundi**.
related: multifarious — the adjective for what a salmagundi is
welter — a mass with no order; salmagundi is the same heap, arranged and served

words.title: Frabjous
words.definition: Delightful; joyous, splendid.
words.etymology: Coined by **Lewis Carroll** for "Jabberwocky" in *Through the Looking-Glass* (published 1871, dated 1872): "O **frabjous** day! Callooh! Callay!" Probably a blend of *fabulous*, *fair*, and *joyous*; Merriam-Webster hedges it as "perhaps alteration of *fabulous*." First documented use: 1872. Carroll glossed several of the poem's coinages through Humpty Dumpty — *slithy*, *mimsy*, *brillig* — but never this one, so the derivation is guesswork by everyone who has tried it since.
words.example: Three days of rain, and then a **frabjous** Saturday that made the whole week worth it.
words.memoryHook: *Fabulous* + *joyous*, run together by Lewis Carroll → **frabjous**. For a day too good for either word on its own.
related: alician — from the same author and the same Looking-Glass world

words.title: Fugacious
words.definition: Literary. Tending to disappear; fleeting, evanescent.
words.etymology: From Latin **fugax**, *fugac-* (apt to flee, fleeting), from *fugere* (to flee), plus *-ious*. First documented use: 1635. The same *fugere* runs under *fugitive*, *refuge*, *subterfuge*, and the musical *fugue*, in which each voice flees the one chasing it. Botanists borrowed the word early for parts of a flower that drop almost as soon as they open.
words.example: Cherry blossom is loved precisely because it is **fugacious** — a week of it, and the street is bare again.
words.memoryHook: *Fugere* = to flee → **fugacious** things run away from you. A *fugitive* flees the law; a fugacious moment flees the person having it.
related: gloaming — the fugacious hour at the end of the day
senescent — what is fugacious vanishes; what is senescent takes its time

words.title: Gloaming
words.definition: Literary. Twilight; dusk.
words.etymology: From Old English **glōmung** (twilight, the fall of evening), from *glōm* (twilight), kin to *glōwan* (to glow) — the gloaming is named for the light that is left, not the dark that is coming. First documented use: before the 12th century. The word then fell out of general English, surviving in Scots and Yorkshire dialect, and re-entered literary English after about 1785 through Robert Burns and the Scottish writers who followed him, which is why it still reads as faintly Scottish. The back-formed noun *gloam* is much later (Keats, 1821). No relation to *gloom*, despite the resemblance.
words.example: They kept walking well into the **gloaming**, until the trail was more memory than sight.
words.memoryHook: *Glōm* (twilight) is kin to *glow* → the **gloaming** is the hour of the afterglow, when the light is leaving but not yet gone.
related: fugacious — the gloaming is the most fugacious hour of the day

words.title: Prolegomenon
words.definition: Prefatory remarks; a formal introductory essay interpreting an extended work.
words.etymology: From Greek **prolegomenon**, "that which is said beforehand" — the neuter passive participle of *prolegein* (to say beforehand), from *pro-* (before) + *legein* (to say). First documented use: 1600. The plural *prolegomena* is the commoner form and is often treated as a singular, largely on the strength of Kant's *Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics* (1783). The same *legein* sits under *prologue*, *lexicon*, and *dialect*.
words.example: What he called a preface ran to ninety pages and was in truth a **prolegomenon** to the entire series.
words.memoryHook: *Pro-* (before) + *legein* (to say) → **prolegomenon** = the saying-before. A prologue with footnotes.
related: indite — the act of composing the thing a prolegomenon introduces
verso — another term from the anatomy of the book
